name: Jalal ad-Din Rumi
bio:
Jalal ad-Din Muhammad was born in 1207 in the town of Wakhsh, then part of the wider Persian-speaking province of Balkh — in what is now Tajikistan, near the border of Afghanistan. His father, Baha ud-Din Walad, was a respected theologian and mystic. When Rumi was a child, the family left ahead of the advancing Mongol armies, traveling west for years through Persia, Baghdad, and Mecca before finally settling in Konya, in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum — Anatolia, in present-day Turkey. It is this adopted home that gave him the name history remembers him by: Rumi, 'the man from Rum.'

By his late thirties, Rumi had inherited his father's position as a respected jurist and theologian, teaching law and preaching to large congregations. Then, in 1244, an encounter changed the course of his life and of Persian literature: a wandering, unconventional mystic named Shams-e Tabrizi arrived in Konya. What passed between the two men — teacher and disciple, or two seekers meeting as equals — is described only in fragments and legend, but its effect is not in doubt. The precise, careful scholar gave way to an ecstatic poet. When Shams disappeared a few years later, Rumi's grief did not end in silence; it opened into tens of thousands of lines of verse, gathered as the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi — a body of work Rumi signed not with his own name, but with the name of the friend he had lost, as if the poems belonged to their union rather than to him alone.

In his last dozen years, Rumi dictated the Masnavi-ye Ma'navi to his scribe and companion Hussam al-Din Chalabi — six books and some 25,000 couplets, composed as a patient, wandering guide to the Sufi path through parable, argument, and story. Generations of readers have called it 'the Quran in Persian' for the way it circles the same handful of truths: that the soul is in exile, that love is the road home, and that the divine can be found nearer than a person's own breath. Rumi died in Konya on the 17th of December, 1273 — a date his followers still mark not as a day of mourning but as his shab-e arus, his 'wedding night,' the moment of union with the Beloved he had spent a lifetime writing toward. He founded no order in his own lifetime; that task fell to his son, Sultan Walad, who organized Rumi's students into what became the Mevlevi order, and formalized the turning prayer — the sema — into the practice known today as the whirling dervishes.

Rumi's message resists easy summary, which may be part of why it has traveled so far beyond its own century and language: that love, not law, is the shortest road to God; that every religion is a different language spoken toward the same truth; that the wound is also the doorway. Eight centuries on, he is read at weddings and funerals, quoted across the world, and remains one of the best-read poets in the English language — a Persian mystic still teaching readers who will never see Konya how to listen for what the reed is grieving. This collection is offered in that spirit: not as the final word on Rumi, which no single collection could be, but as a doorway in.
